claims.text: The addition of a dominated decoy option can influence choices without forbidding options, behaving as a nudge.
Conditions making a nudge easy and cheap to avoid, specifically transparency and deliberation-triggering, are often violated.
Nudges can be defined as interventions attempting to influence behavior by exploiting, at least in part, rationality failures and that do not increase, exclusively, the well-being of nudgers.
Libertarian paternalism justifies pro-self nudges but does not justify pro-social or commercial nudges.
Transparent default nudges do not diminish their effectiveness and can in some cases enhance compliance.
In retirement savings, active decision nudges yielded a return of $100 per dollar invested compared to approximately $15 for retirement savings information policies.
For influenza vaccination, a planning-prompt nudge yielded approximately 13 adults vaccinated per $100 spent versus 9 for an educational campaign.
Introducing green nudges can crowd out public support for carbon tax policies.
A nudge to promote retirement saving does not affect support for carbon taxes.

evidence.description: Kivetz et al. (2004) and Ariely (2009) demonstrated that adding a decoy option in journal subscription offerings shifted choices toward the more expensive option.
Many nudges target automatic System 1 processes rather than reflective System 2 processes and are non-transparent in existence, workings, or intention.
The authors propose synthesising Hansen's narrow definition with a non-exclusive well-being clause to distinguish nudges from traditional interventions and exploitative marketing.
Libertarian paternalism authorizes policies making individuals better off as judged by themselves, whereas pro-social nudges primarily benefit society or third parties.

Bruns et al. (2018) showed no statistically significant differences in donations between transparent and non-transparent defaults, while Paunov et al. (2019) found higher compliance when the default was disclosed.
Benartzi et al. (2017) calculated impact per dollar comparing active decision nudges to Duflo & Saez's (2003) retirement benefits fair information intervention.
Benartzi et al. (2017) evaluated Milkman et al. (2011) against Kimura et al. (2007) and found 13 vaccinations per $100 for the planning prompt versus 9 for the educational campaign.
Werfel (2017) and Hagmann et al. (2019) experimentally observed that introducing green nudges decreased subjects' support for carbon tax policies.
Hagmann et al. (2019) found that while retirement nudges reduced social security tax support, they did not diminish carbon tax support.

methodologies.name: Literature review and conceptual synthesis
methodologies.description: A comprehensive interdisciplinary narrative review synthesizing research on definitions, normative justifications, and empirical effectiveness of nudging.
conditions: Focus on justifications (libertarian paternalism vs alternatives)
Focus on empirical effectiveness and policy interactions

limitations.text: The proposed definition clauses 'at least in part' and 'not exclusively' make the definition somewhat indefinite because verifying whether they are satisfied is not always straightforward.
Evidence regarding whether transparency hampers effectiveness is largely limited to default nudges and lacks systematic empirical evidence across other nudge types.
There is insufficient evidence to confidently state whether or when Type 1 nudges produce sustained behavioral changes over time.

future_work.text: Investigate to what extent the preservation of effectiveness under transparent disclosure applies to nudges other than default options.
Assess additional variables influencing long-term nudge effectiveness, including credibility of information source, specificity of targeted behavior, and strength of prior preferences and habits.
